data.content_ref: inline:The target answers the cross-city part of the question with a latent-cooling modulator (green space/irrigation), but this predicts the wrong direction for the largest nocturnal gaps. The largest, most robust nocturnal UHIs occur in dry, desert cities (e.g., Phoenix), and the target itself says arid, heavily-impervious cities are 'more pronounced' because they lack a latent sink. Yet the same arid climate also makes the countryside lack evapotranspiration, so the rural-urban latent differential should collapse there, not widen. Conversely, the cross-city literature documents that the nocturnal gap is typically LARGEST in humid-temperate cities, where rural evapotranspiration is substantial and daytime urban evapotranspiration is suppressed — the opposite of the stated 'humid = smaller gap' claim. The latent-heat framing is therefore internally contradictory: it cannot simultaneously justify arid cities as having the largest gaps (because imperviousness removes cooling) and humid cities as having smaller gaps, because the arid rural baseline has no latent sink to create the differential in the first place. The dominant observed cross-city modulator of nocturnal UHI is the urban canyon geometry (sky-view factor / building-height-to-street-width ratio) controlling longwave radiative trapping, which the target subordinates to latent heat.
